newsitem.title: UK: Buoyant stg asset-backed Eurobonds await NatWest.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant stg asset-backed Eurobonds await NatWest.

text.p: The sterling asset-backed bond market will get a further boost when NatWest launches its jumbo securitisation at the end of the month, traders said on Monday.
"The investor base for sterling securitised paper is constantly broadening, and this trend will continue as new structures are launched," said a head of securitisation at a British bank.
"Many of the deals have targeted different investor bases. At the moment there is still plenty of capacity to place paper with both bank and non-bank investors," he said.

Continuing low interest rates have boosted investor appetite for asset-backed bonds which usually have top-notch ratings but pay extra yield to compensate for the complex structure due to their securitisation.
Securitised bonds are typically backed by income from mortgages or credit cards, although other income streams are also used.
Last week, for instance, Annington Homes issued a deal backed by Ministry of Defence home rental incomes.
The sterling asset-backed Eurobond market is now unrecognisable from a year ago as new issue volumes have rocketed and new structures emerged.
So far this year $9.6 billion equivalent has been launched, compared with a paltry $1.7 billion for the whole of 1995, Capital Data Bondware figures showed.

Last week alone nearly 1.5 billion stg was raised in the sector and NatWest's innovative securitisation of high-quality, low-margin corporate loans will add a further 1.8 billion stg, as well as issue dollar paper.

The NatWest paper, which will be issued by special purpose vehicle R.O.S.E. Funding, has an added difference in that it has an expected double-A rating, in contrast to the more usual triple-A rating of securitised bonds.
Fitch is the only rating agency to have made public its expected rating, but bankers said other agencies were likely to follow with a similar double-A verdict.

"NatWest is passing on the economic interest of the loans but is not changing the legal title. Legally it remains a NatWest loan, so you can't get above NatWest's rating," said a syndicate manager at a British bank.
But the lower rating might boost the deal's appeal.
"There is huge appetite for triple-A asset-backed paper at fine margins," said a bond trader at a European bank.

"I imagine there would be an appetite for a slightly lower rating and higher margins. Now that investors are more familiar with asset-backed bonds, they may be willing to take on some structural risk," he said.
The NatWest issue, which will total around $5.0 billion, will consist of six double-A rated tranches which will have one-, three-, and five-year expected average lives.
There will also be lower-rated bonds.

Dealers said pricing could be at around 10 basis points over Libor for the one-year paper, the high-teens to low-twenties b.p. over Libor for three-year paper and the mid-20 b.p. over Libor for the five-year maturity.
But only half the deal will be placed with end-investors initially, dealers said.
"Half of the deal will be bought by a conduit, R.O.S.E. Inc, and the other half placed with asset-backed bond investors," said a dealer at a European bank.
